holding: The standard governing criminal cases is proof beyond reasonable doubt. The prosecution case must stand on its own legs. As the Supreme Court has repeatedly held, the benefit of every reasonable doubt must go to the accused, not as a matter of concession or grace, but as a matter of right.7 The concurrent findings of the courts below, while ordinarily entitled to deference, are not immune from review in criminal revision where they are perverse, rest on misreading or non-reading of evidence, or involve fundamental errors of law. In the present case, the deficiencies discussed above render the Petitioner’s conviction unsustainable. Accordingly, Crl. Revision No. 383/J/2025 is allowed. The conviction and sentence of the Petitioner are set aside, and he is acquitted of the charge. He shall be released from jail forthwith if he is not required to be detained in any other case. (Tariq Saleem Sheikh) Judge Naeem

paragraphs.text: Date of hearing 12.05.2026 For the Petitioner: Barrister Muhammad Yar Khan Dah, assisted by Mr. Junaid Fareed Khan Dah, Advocate, and Mr. Sohail Khan Chadhar, Defence Counsel. For the State: Rana Tasawar Ali Khan, Additional Prosecutor General. For the Informant: Rao Muhammad Azeem Liaquat, Advocate. Tariq Saleem Sheikh, J. – On 08.10.2019, Sakina Bibi (PW-1) submitted an application (Exh. PA), forwarded by the Regional Police Officer, Sahiwal Region, to Muhammad Younas/ASI (PW-3) at Adda Chakbedi, Pakpattan, for registration of an FIR. According to that application, on 12.03.2019 at about 12:00 noon, she and her family members were engaged in sorting and collecting potatoes in an agricultural field at Chakbedi, Pakpattan. During the course of work, her daughter-in-law, Kalsoom Bibi, placed her minor daughter, Haikal Bibi, aged about two years, on the edge (wat) of the field. Meanwhile, the Petitioner allegedly arrived at the spot driving a tractor at high speed and ran over the child, who died. According to Sakina Bibi, he concealed the body beneath empty sacks. Later, when she and Kalsoom Bibi completed their work and could not find the child, they began searching for her. Their cries attracted Muhammad Din, Allah Ditta, and other villagers. Haikal’s body was ultimately recovered from beneath the sacks in their presence. Muhammad Younas/ASI (PW-3) made his endorsement on the said application and sent it to the Police Station Chakbedi, District Pakpattan, through Muhammad Ashraf 96/C. Muhammad Irfan Mehmood 31/HC (PW-4) registered FIR No. 471/2019 (Exh. PE) on that basis.

The case was investigated, and the Petitioner was challaned to the court. On 06.10.2020, the Senior Civil Judge (Criminal Division), Pakpattan, indicted him under section 322 PPC. He pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.

To prove the charge, the prosecution examined six witnesses. Sakina Bibi (PW-1) and Allah Ditta (PW-2) were produced as witnesses of the occurrence. Muhammad Younas/ASI (PW-3) gave the details of the investigation and the evidence collected during it. Muhammad Irfan Mehmood 31/HC (PW-4) registered the FIR. Muhammad Abbas 665/C (PW-5) testified about the taking into possession of a copy of driving licence No. DN-19-1569 from the Petitioner by the Investigating Officer through Recovery Memo Exh. PD. Dr. Saleha Ayub (PW-6) furnished the medical evidence. The public prosecutor gave up PW Muhammad Din, as he had died, and closed the prosecution evidence after tendering the forensic report Exh. PH and the licence verification certificate Exh. PI.

After the prosecution completed its evidence, the trial court recorded the Petitioner’s statement under section 342 Cr.P.C. and confronted him with the incriminating evidence brought against him. He denied the allegations and professed innocence. He stated that he had been implicated in the case to blackmail him. The Petitioner neither opted to make a statement on oath under section 340(2) Cr.P.C. nor produced any witness in his defence.

Upon conclusion of the trial, vide judgment dated 11.06.2024, the Senior Civil Judge (Criminal Division), Pakpattan, convicted the Petitioner under section 322 PPC and sentenced him to pay diyat amounting to Rs. 20,55,936/-, payable to the legal heirs of the deceased, Haikal Bibi. He was ordered to remain in custody until payment of diyat. The Petitioner challenged his conviction and sentence in appeal, which was dismissed by the Additional Sessions Judge, Pakpattan, vide judgment dated 07.11.2024. Aggrieved, he has filed the instant criminal revision before this Court.

Barrister Muhammad Yar Khan Dah contended that the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. He submitted that the courts below had not properly appreciated the evidence, which caused a serious miscarriage of justice. He argued that the Petitioner had been falsely implicated and that the prosecution had not established that any tractor driven by him had hit the child. The FIR was lodged with an unexplained delay of six months and 26 days, which, according to him, reflected adversely on the credibility of the prosecution version. He submitted that it was a case of no evidence. Neither Sakina Bibi (PW-1) nor Allah Ditta (PW-2) had witnessed the occurrence. Kalsoom Bibi, mother of the deceased and the most natural witness, was not produced at the trial. Counsel further submitted that the body was exhumed after several months in a skeletonised condition, and it was not satisfactorily proved that the remains were those of Haikal Bibi. No X-ray or other radiological examination was conducted, nor was any DNA test performed. He, therefore, prayed for the Petitioner’s acquittal.

The Additional Prosecutor General supported the concurrent findings of the courts below. He contended that the delay in registration of the FIR was fully explained. He argued that the Petitioner had used his influence to prevent registration, which compelled Sakina Bibi to approach the Regional Police Officer, Sahiwal Region, on whose direction FIR No. 471/2019 (Exh. PE) was eventually registered. He contended that the prosecution evidence, taken as a whole, inspired confidence and was sufficient to sustain the conviction. On the question of identification, he argued that the exhumation and postmortem examination had been conducted in accordance with law and that the identity of the deceased had been duly proved. He prayed for dismissal of the revision.

Counsel for the Informant, Rao Azeem Liaquat, Advocate, adopted the APG’s submissions. He added that the Petitioner drove the tractor at high speed, ran over the child, and thereafter concealed her body beneath empty sacks. He further submitted that the Petitioner did not have a valid driving licence at the time of the occurrence, which constituted the unlawful act required by section 321 PPC. He also prayed for dismissal of the revision.
Arguments heard. Record perused.

The Petitioner is accused of an offence under section 322 PPC. Section 321 PPC defines qatl-bis-sabab as follows: “Whoever, without any intention to cause death of, or cause harm to, any person, does any unlawful act which becomes a cause for the death of another person, is said to commit qatl-bis-sabab.” Section 322 PPC prescribes diyat as the punishment therefor. The ingredients of qatl-bis-sabab, therefore, are: (i) that the accused committed an act; (ii) that such act was unlawful; (iii) that the accused had no intention to cause death or bodily harm; and (iv) that the unlawful act became a cause of the death of another person. Each ingredient must be proved beyond reasonable doubt.

The prosecution case against the Petitioner is based on the testimony of Sakina Bibi (PW-1) and Allah Ditta (PW-2), medical and forensic evidence, and the recovery of tractor bearing registration No. SLS-1229. Sakina Bibi (PW-1), however, admitted during cross- examination that when the tractor allegedly struck the child, she was unaware of it. According to her, Kalsoom Bibi later found the child dead and raised cries, whereafter she and Allah Ditta came to the spot. This admission weakens the prosecution version, as it shows that Sakina Bibi (PW-1) did not see the tractor hitting the child. It also accords with the defence contention that none of the persons produced at the trial had witnessed the occurrence.

Allah Ditta (PW-2), father of the deceased, deposed that the field comprised about 25 acres, that the potato crop was being harvested through tractors, and that labourers were picking potatoes. He further stated that his wife had laid Haikal Bibi down along the wat of the field. They worked for about two hours, after which they found her dead. His claim to have been present and at work throughout, however, cannot be reconciled with the account of Sakina Bibi (PW-1), according to whom he arrived at the spot only after hearing Kalsoom Bibi’s cries. The two prosecution witnesses thus differ even as to whether PW-2 was present at the relevant time. In addition, several important assertions made by Allah Ditta (PW-2) at the trial were not found in his previous statement recorded under section 161 Cr.P.C. (Exh. DA), including the allegation that the Petitioner had intentionally driven the tractor over her and thereafter placed empty sacks upon the body. These omissions relate to the essential particulars of the occurrence and materially impair the credibility of his account. It is well settled that a witness who makes such improvements, particularly where they appear to strengthen the prosecution case, cannot be regarded as reliable.1

The cross-examination of Muhammad Younas/ASI (PW-3), the Investigating Officer, is even more significant. He admitted that the complainant party did not initially suspect the commission of any offence and buried the body after the funeral rites. He also admitted that the Petitioner was not named at the outset. According to his investigation, labourers were working in the field and some drivers were digging potatoes with tillers. The child had been placed among potato plants by her mother. None of the drivers knew that she was lying there. He further stated that his investigation revealed that none of the drivers had intentionally driven the tractor over her, and that Sakina Bibi (PW-1) and other persons were not close to the child at the time of the occurrence.

The most important witness in this case was Kalsoom Bibi, the mother of the deceased minor, who, according to the prosecution, was present with Haikal Bibi at the relevant time. She was the person who had placed the child along the wat of the field and was also the first to find her dead. Despite this, she was not examined at the trial. Her non-production warrants an adverse inference under Illustration (g) to section 129 of the Qanun-e-Shahadat, 1984. It is a settled principle that where the best available evidence is withheld without a satisfactory explanation, the court is entitled to presume that it would, if produced, have been unfavourable to the party withholding it.2 Kalsoom Bibi’s non-production assumes added significance because, as discussed above, the witnesses produced at the trial had not seen the actual impact.

The delay in lodging the FIR is another circumstance that casts doubt on the prosecution’s case. The alleged occurrence took place on 12.03.2019 and the FIR was registered on 08.10.2019, after six months and 26 days. The prosecution sought to explain this delay by reference to alleged pressure from the accused party and initial police inaction. However, these assertions were not supported by any evidence apart from the bare statement 1 Ibrar Hussain and others v. The State and another (2007 SCMR 605). 2 Riaz Ahmed v. State (PLJ 2010 SC 877), Akhtar Ali and others v. The State (2008 SCMR 6), Muhammad Rafique and others v. The State and others (2010 SCMR 385), Muhammad Naeem Inayat v. The State (2010 SCMR 1054), Muhammad Saleem v. Muhammad Azan and another (2011 SCMR 474), Sardar Bibi and another v. Munir Ahmed and others (2017 SCMR 344). of Sakina Bibi (PW-1). Importantly, the complainant party initially buried the body without any accusation against any person, and the Petitioner was named only after the aforementioned interval. This sequence of events, combined with the Investigating Officer’s evidence that none of the drivers was initially suspected of intentional wrongdoing, affords a legitimate basis for doubting whether the accusation against the Petitioner was the product of subsequent deliberation and consultation.

The prosecution heavily relied on the recovery of tractor No. SLS-1229 to connect the Petitioner with the occurrence. Muhammad Younas/ASI (PW-3) stated that he took the tractor into possession on 08.10.2019 vide Recovery Memo Exh. PB. However, the tractor in question was not produced at the trial. Nor was any mechanical inspection, physical mark, forensic link, tyre pattern, blood trace, tissue material, or other independent circumstance brought on record to connect the said tractor with the death of the child. Such corroboration was essential because the field was large and more than one driver was working there. In these circumstances, Exh. PB could prove, at the highest, that tractor No. SLS-1229 was taken into possession during the investigation. It could not establish that it was the same vehicle that struck Haikal Bibi.

The prosecution was obligated to prove that the body exhumed and examined was that of Haikal Bibi. The Petitioner has specifically challenged the identity of the exhumed remains and the probative worth of the postmortem examination conducted after several months, when the body was in a partially skeletonised condition. It is, therefore, necessary to examine the legal framework governing exhumation and the evidentiary value of a postmortem conducted in such circumstances.

The legal framework governing exhumation is found principally in sections 174 and 176 Cr.P.C., read with Rule 25.34 of the Punjab Police Rules, 1934, and Chapter 18, Part A, Rules 2 and 3 of Volume III of the Rules and Orders of the Lahore High Court, Lahore. Section 174 Cr.P.C. requires the police officer, upon receiving information of an unnatural or suspicious death, to proceed to the place where the body is found, hold an inquest in the presence of two or more respectable inhabitants of the neighbourhood, and prepare a report stating the apparent cause of death and the nature of wounds, fractures, bruises or other marks of injury. Where there is doubt regarding the cause of death, section 174(3) Cr.P.C. contemplates medical examination by a Civil Surgeon or other qualified medical officer appointed in that behalf. Section 176(2) Cr.P.C. empowers the Magistrate, where he considers it expedient for discovering the cause of death, to cause an already buried body to be disinterred and examined. Rule 25.34 of the Police Rules supplements the above provisions. It requires the investigating police officer to record the information received and the grounds for seeking disinterment, forward them to the nearest Magistrate empowered to hold inquests with a request for an order under section 176(2) Cr.P.C., guard the grave in the meantime, and, upon receipt of such order, cause the body to be disinterred in the presence of two or more respectable inhabitants if the Magistrate does not himself attend. It further requires that, after disinterment, the procedure prescribed by section 174 Cr.P.C. be followed and witnesses be examined to establish the identity of the body before the investigation proceeds. Where the body has been buried for more than three weeks, Rule 25.34 contains an additional safeguard requiring the opinion of the District Health Officer and the concurrence of the District Magistrate. Chapter 18, Part A, Rules 2 and 3 of Volume III of the Rules and Orders of the Lahore High Court address the circumstances in which a postmortem examination should be conducted and the considerations that should guide the Magistrate in deciding whether to order exhumation. In cases of doubt, the Magistrate should, if possible, consult a medical officer before passing such order. These provisions collectively show that, in a case of exhumation, proof of the identity of the body, the medical utility of the examination, and the integrity of the proceedings are matters of substance, not empty form.

Apart from the above provisions, the leading textbooks of medical jurisprudence and forensic medicine set out certain procedural safeguards which reflect accepted standards of medico-legal practice. These works do not have statutory force, but courts in Pakistan and other common law jurisdictions have often treated them as useful guides while evaluating medico-legal evidence.

Modi3 states that, as a matter of procedure, before digging the grave, the police should examine the plan of the graveyard, if available, to fix the exact location of the grave. Upon reaching the place, the nameplate (grave marker), if any, should be noted, and the caretaker of the graveyard or another person familiar with the grave, such as a grave-digger, should be asked to identify it. The grave should then be dug up, and the coffin, if present, should be identified by a person who attended or supervised the burial. The coffin or body should then be raised from the grave, and the identity of the body should be confirmed by as many persons as possible, particularly relatives, friends or servants who may have been present when the body was prepared and dressed for burial. According to the author, where a body is buried illegally, it is invariably placed in a shallow grave and is liable to greater decomposition, depending on the weather.

Modi further states that, where the interment has been recent, the postmortem examination should be conducted in the usual manner, either in the open near the graveyard, screened from public gaze, or at the mortuary. Where a body has remained buried for a sufficiently long period and undergone putrefaction, an attempt should be made to determine the sex, stature and marks of identification. A photograph of the exhumed body may help in identification. If necessary, an X-ray examination of the cadaver should be undertaken. Hair found on the body should be preserved in a dry, clean glass bottle for subsequent identification and chemical analysis. A search should be made for recent or old injuries, such as fractures. The body should be examined as fully as its condition permits, and appropriate specimens should be preserved and forwarded to the forensic science laboratory.

Parikh,4 Taylor,5 and Aggrawal6 take a similar view, but add certain details relevant to the reliability of an exhumation. Parikh emphasises that the grave should be identified from cemetery records and by persons who attended the burial. He further states that the exhumation should be conducted under medical and police supervision, that the body 3 Modi, A Textbook of Medical Jurisprudence and Toxicology, 27th ed., p. 382 (LexisNexis) 4 Parikh’s Textbook of Medical Jurisprudence and Toxicology, p. 128 5 Taylor, Principles and Practice of Medical Jurisprudence, 13th ed., p. 17 6 Anil Aggrawal’s Textbook of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, p. 7 should be photographed where appropriate, that the medical officer should have the complete history of the case, and that bone fractures, especially in decomposed bodies, should be carefully distinguished from damage caused during digging or from normal anatomical features in children. Taylor adds that attendance at the exhumation should be restricted to persons having a duty to perform, that privacy should be preserved, that the coffin and body should preferably be examined at a mortuary where practicable, and that the pathologist should ensure, before re-burial, that all necessary material has been collected because later re-examination may not be possible. Aggrawal further notes that, where the body is skeletonised, the remains should be recovered carefully and the surrounding earth should be sifted so that smaller bones, teeth and associated objects are not lost.

The above safeguards ensure that the body exhumed is properly identified, that the remains are recovered without avoidable loss or contamination, that injuries are examined by a competent medical officer in light of the condition of the body, and that relevant material is preserved for further analysis. The reliability of the process depends upon these matters.

There are very few reported cases in Pakistan on the procedure to be followed after a Magistrate orders exhumation. Even the available cases deal only with particular aspects of that process. In Muhammad Rafique alias Feeqa v. The State (2019 SCMR 1068), the Supreme Court did not deal directly with exhumation, but explained the procedure regarding postmortem examination where a person has died in unnatural or suspicious circumstances. The Court held that once the police take charge of the dead body, it remains under their control until it is handed over to the relatives or, where they are unknown, until burial. It further held that a postmortem examination must be authorised by a competent police officer or Magistrate, conducted by a notified government Medical Officer, and accompanied by the relevant police papers prepared during the investigation. In Abdul Ghani v. 1st Judicial Magistrate, Tando Adam, and others (2018 PCr.LJ 1455), the Sindh High Court held that where the identity of an unknown body was in dispute and photographic identification was not satisfactory, exhumation and DNA testing were necessary to resolve the issue. In Muhammad Tayyab and another v. The State and others (2023 YLR 2207), this Court treated failure to prove the identity of a skeleton, absence of a reliable medical opinion as to the time and cause of death, and a broken chain of custody of forensic evidence as serious infirmities. In Sawab Khan v. The State and another (2024 MLD 1682), the Peshawar High Court found the exhumation proceedings reliable because the graves and the bodies had been duly identified, the relevant memos had been prepared and attested, and the proceedings had been conducted in the presence of responsible officers, an Executive Magistrate, and a medical team. These cases, read together, support a limited but important principle: where the prosecution relies upon an exhumed body, it must prove the identity of the body, the lawful authorisation and proper supervision of the examination, and the integrity of the medico-legal examination and, where relevant, the forensic chain of custody.

Having regard to the legal provisions, the medico-legal literature and case law discussed above, the following procedure should ideally be followed for exhumation: First, the exhumation must be carried out pursuant to an order of a competent Magistrate. Secondly, the grave and the body must be identified through reliable evidence, including, where available, cemetery records and the testimony of persons who attended the burial, relatives, or other persons capable of identifying the grave or the body. Thirdly, the disinterment should be conducted in the presence of responsible officers and respectable inhabitants of the locality, unless the circumstances justify departure. Fourthly, the medical examination must be conducted by a competent medical officer with due regard to the condition of the body and the nature of the suspected injury. Fifthly, where the body is decomposed or skeletonised, relevant material, including bones, teeth, hair, nails, clothing or associated articles, should be carefully preserved for scientific examination, where necessary. Sixthly, the chain of custody of the remains and samples must be properly documented. Throughout the exhumation, due regard must be had to the dignity of the dead body and the privacy of the proceedings. I may add that unauthorised photography, videography or recording should not be allowed, and that no images or videos of the exhumation should be uploaded or circulated on social media. No information or findings arising out of the exhumation should be disclosed to the media or any member of the public, and all matters relating to the exhumation should be treated as confidential until the competent court permits otherwise.

The above guidelines are not a rigid statutory code. They may be departed from where the circumstances so require. Furthermore, not every irregularity in the exhumation proceedings will, by itself, vitiate the prosecution case. The decisive question is whether the departure or omission affects proof of identity, the reliability of the medical opinion, or the integrity of the medico-legal examination.

Considering the above principles, the prosecution in this case was required to prove that the exhumation proceedings were conducted under lawful authority and with sufficient safeguards, that the remains examined were those of Haikal Bibi, and that the cause of death was reliably established by the medical evidence. The record must now be examined against these requirements.

Dr. Saleha Ayub (PW-6) deposed that on 26.10.2019 she received a written order from the Medical Superintendent, DHQ Hospital, Pakpattan, and that she, along with supporting staff, reached the graveyard at Chakbedi Khurd in compliance with the order of the Area Magistrate. She further stated that a body described as that of Haikal Bibi was disinterred on that date. The record, however, does not show that any independent witness of the locality was examined to prove the identity of the grave or the body at the time of disinterment. Nor was any witness produced who had been present at the burial and could identify the grave or the remains with certainty. This omission is significant because Rule 25.34 of the Punjab Police Rules requires that witnesses be examined to prove the identity of the disinterred body before the investigation proceeds. It was not merely procedural but went to the proof of a foundational fact upon which the evidentiary value of the postmortem examination depended.

A more serious issue concerns the identity of the skeletal remains. Dr. Saleha Ayub (PW-6) stated in examination-in-chief that she observed a partially skeletonised body of a female child with hair and nails. However, in cross-examination, she admitted that the dead body was unidentifiable. She further stated that the relatives of the deceased did not point out any symbol or mark of identification to her and that she was “not sure” whether the skeleton examined by her was that of Haikal Bibi. This admission goes to the root of the matter. Although the postmortem report (Exh. PG) described the remains as those of “Haikel Bibi (Aital Bibi) d/o Allah Ditta”, the record does not show the basis upon which that description was recorded. No DNA report, odontological evidence, distinctive article, identifying mark, or reliable testimony of a burial witness was produced.

The courts below treated the identity of the skeletal remains as duly proved. The trial court proceeded on the premise that the remains were those of Haikal Bibi. The appellate court likewise observed that the Medical Officer had identified the skeleton as that of a female child aged about two years and that Sakina Bibi (PW-1) had identified the grave. That approach is unsafe. Identification of sex and approximate age is not the same as proof that the skeleton belonged to Haikal Bibi. At most, the medical evidence showed that the remains were of a female child of about two years. It did not establish that they were the remains of Haikal Bibi.

The medical evidence regarding the cause of death also suffers from serious deficiencies. In her examination-in-chief, Dr. Saleha Ayub (PW-6) deposed that she found a fracture at the base of the skull on the right side, involving the right occipital and temporal bones. She initially reserved her opinion, stating that she would give it after receiving the PFSA report. She later stated that the most likely cause of death was brain stem injury. Her cross-examination, however, materially undermined this conclusion. She conceded that the time of death could not be determined and that the intervals between injury and death, and between death and postmortem examination, were unassessable. More importantly, she acknowledged that she had not received the final PFSA report and could not formulate a final opinion without it. Her evidence as to the cause of death was, therefore, internally inconsistent.

The absence of radiological examination is particularly significant in this context. Dr. Saleha Ayub (PW-6) admitted that no radiologist accompanied her to the graveyard at the time of disinterment and postmortem and that no X-ray was conducted. She further admitted that the fracture could be determined only through an X-ray. This admission casts serious doubt on the finding of a fracture, which she had recorded upon examination of partially skeletonised remains without radiological confirmation. She also stated that a simple fracture could not cause death unless it resulted in consequential injury, but no such injury was observed in the present case. Although an X-ray may not be necessary in every exhumation case, its omission was material here because the body was partially skeletonised and the alleged fatal injury was a fracture.

The PFSA report Exh. PH did not help the prosecution in establishing either the identity of the remains or the cause of death. It records that five sealed jars containing the radius, ulna, nail, femur, skull bone, hair and teeth were received. However, the examination was confined to toxicological analysis of the hair for specified drugs. No DNA analysis was conducted, and the report merely concluded that the specified drugs were not detected in the hair.

The custody of the samples was also not fully accounted for. Dr. Saleha Ayub (PW-6) stated that the samples were collected during postmortem on 26.10.2019 and handed over to the police in sealed parcels. Muhammad Younas/ASI (PW-3), however, stated that he received five sealed parcels from the Medical Officer on 30.10.2019 and deposited them with PFSA on the following day. The record does not explain who retained custody of the samples during the intervening period. In a case where the body had been exhumed after several months and was in a partially skeletonised condition, strict proof of the chain of custody was of particular importance.

Notably, the prosecution failed to establish a causal link between the Petitioner’s alleged act and the death. The courts below treated the absence of a valid driving licence as the unlawful act required by section 321 PPC. Even if that view is accepted, the prosecution was still required to prove beyond reasonable doubt that the Petitioner was driving the tractor which struck Haikal Bibi and that such driving caused her death. These foundational facts were not proved. As discussed, no eyewitness, physical mark, forensic link, mechanical inspection, or other independent circumstance connected tractor No. SLS-1229 with the occurrence.

The prosecution alleged that the Petitioner sought forgiveness from the bereaved family after the occurrence and helped in the funeral arrangements of the deceased. The courts below treated this conduct as an incriminating circumstance. However, such conduct was equally consistent with sympathy for the family or a sense of communal solidarity. It could not bridge the evidentiary gap or substitute for proof beyond reasonable doubt.

The standard governing criminal cases is proof beyond reasonable doubt. The prosecution case must stand on its own legs. As the Supreme Court has repeatedly held, the benefit of every reasonable doubt must go to the accused, not as a matter of concession or grace, but as a matter of right.7 The concurrent findings of the courts below, while ordinarily entitled to deference, are not immune from review in criminal revision where they are perverse, rest on misreading or non-reading of evidence, or involve fundamental errors of law. In the present case, the deficiencies discussed above render the Petitioner’s conviction unsustainable. Accordingly, Crl. Revision No. 383/J/2025 is allowed. The conviction and sentence of the Petitioner are set aside, and he is acquitted of the charge. He shall be released from jail forthwith if he is not required to be detained in any other case. (Tariq Saleem Sheikh) Judge Naeem Approved for reporting Judge 7 Tariq Pervez v. The State (1995 SCMR 1345) and Muhammad Akram v. The State (2009 SCMR 230).
